title: Only closeness (8:2)
hook: Maimonides pictures the world to come without bodies, a life of knowing God
tomorrow: then why does the Torah keep promising rain and harvests?

segments.voice: Yesterday: let them be new. No reminding, not even as a joke. Today the laws look much further ahead, past this life altogether.

Physical therapy, week whatever. The knee won't bend, the back complains, the stairs feel taller than they used to. Somewhere in the middle of it, people say things like: well, in heaven I'll get a new one. Do we bring our bodies? Maimonides has a surprising answer for the world to come, olam haba. There aren't any.
screen: `THE KNEE WON'T BEND.` → `IN HEAVEN, A NEW ONE?` → `OLAM HABA: NO BODIES.`

segments.voice: In the world to come, he writes, there is no body and no bodily form, only the souls of the righteous, without bodies, like the angels. No eating, no drinking, none of what bodies need. He quotes the sages of the Talmud: in the world to come there is no eating and no drinking, but the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah, the divine presence. Then he explains the crown. It isn't gold. It's the knowing they reached in this life. And to enjoy the radiance means to know and grasp God in a way they couldn't while in a body. So the picture isn't a buffet and a better knee. It's nearness. Only closeness. Here's what's worth saying at dinner: for Maimonides, the reward for a life of turning toward God isn't more stuff. It's the turning, finally complete. Two honest notes. Jewish thinkers don't all paint it this way; Nachmanides, for one, pictured the world to come with bodies restored. And Maimonides himself, in other writings, also affirms the resurrection of the dead; how the two fit is a question his readers still ask. The tradition holds the argument open. What it keeps, across the argument, is where the road ends: near God.
screen: `NO BODY, NO FOOD, NO DRINK.` · `CROWNS AND THE RADIANCE.` · `THE CROWN IS WHAT THEY KNEW.` · `NACHMANIDES SAW BODIES RESTORED.` · then, large: `NO BODY, ONLY CLOSENESS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the body be what it is: the ache, the itch, the weight in the chair. Without fighting any of it, bring to mind someone you love being near you, not doing anything, just near. Stay with that nearness until the bell.
Only closeness: Maimonides' picture of the world to come. No bodies, no food; the righteous knowing God.
Hold this one: no body, only closeness, where the reward is nearness itself. Day twenty-two, complete.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition speaks of olam haba, the world to come, in more than one way; Jews study Maimonides' bodiless picture alongside other views, and the resurrection of the dead is named in the daily Amidah prayer.

chat.says: Saba after PT: 'in the world to come, a brand new hip!' is that what we actually believe??
options: Maimonides says no bodies there, only closeness to God. Others, like Nachmanides, saw bodies restored.
Yes. Every Jewish source agrees the world to come is this world, healthier and well fed.
No. Jewish tradition says nothing at all about after death, so Saba's just joking.
chat.meaning: Maimonides pictures the world to come without bodies, only nearness to God; Nachmanides and others pictured bodies restored.

Nachmanides.meaning: a Jewish sage who pictured the world to come with bodies

Maimonides.meaning: a Jewish sage and legal scholar; he wrote the Mishneh Torah

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 8:2 (no body or bodily form in the world to come; the souls of the righteous like angels; the crowns are knowledge; enjoying the radiance is knowing God)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (no eating or drinking; the righteous sit with crowns and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah)
